newsitem.title: USA: Justice Dept. urges FCC to deny Ameritech phone bid.
newsitem.headline: Justice Dept. urges FCC to deny Ameritech phone bid.

text.p: The Justice Department urged federal phone regulators Wednesday to reject Ameritech Corp.'s bid to offer long-distance phone service in Michigan.

The recommendation to the Federal Communications Commission is a major blow to Chicago-based Ameritech's effort to enter the $80 billion long-distance business by offering service from its local-calling region.
The department said the Baby Bell had made "important progress" in opening its local phone network in Michigan to competitors, such as long-distance companies and cable-television operators.
But the Chicago-based carrier had not gone far enough to satisfy the requirements of last year's communications law, the department contended.

Under the law, a Baby Bell can offer long-distance phoning from its own region once the FCC rules the carrier has met a 14-point checklist of requirements for opening its local network. The Bells have yet to win such approval.

The law requires the FCC to give "substantial weight" to the Justice Department's recommendation. Last month, the department urged the FCC to reject SBC Communications Inc.'s application to offer long-distance service in Oklahoma.

"As a result of Ameritech's efforts and cooperation with the department, as well as the state of Michigan's leadership in removing legal and economic barriers to entry, local competition is beginning to take root in Michigan," Acting Assistant Attorney General Joel Klein said in a statement.
But Klein added that Ameritech had not yet fully met the checklist and that the company has not yet demonstrated that "its markets are fully and irreversibly open to competition."
The department cited shortcomings related to a competitor being able to direct the routing of local calls.
The department also found, among other things, that calls between an Ameritech customer and a competitor's customer were blocked more often than calls between two Ameritech customers.

"Ameritech has jumped the gun with its ... application. Until Michigan's residential and business customers can enjoy the benefits of more choices, lower prices and better service, the FCC should reject Ameritech's premature bid," MCI Communications Corp. attorney Jonathan Sallet said.

Ameritech asked the FCC on May 21 for permission to offer long-distance service in Michigan, one of the five Midwestern states in which the company provides local calling. The FCC is scheduled to make a final decision by August 19.
Ameritech has 3.5 million customers in Michigan. The carrier values the long-distance market in its five-state territory at about $9 billion a year.
Earlier this year Ameritech was forced to withdraw its initial long-distance application because of numerous errors.
Meanwhile, the FCC is expected soon to rule on SBC's application to offer long-distance service, following the Justice Department's recommendation that it reject the bid.
Analysts expect the FCC to follow that advice.
